WEEK 2A · RELATIONAL VOCABULARY, KEYS, AND DATA INDEPENDENCE

# Why use this abstract language at all?

The relational model gives us a precise way to describe data, relationships, and identifiers without tying those descriptions to one file layout, pointer structure, or access algorithm. That precision is the point: we want a stable language for saying what data means before we talk about how a system stores or traverses it.

::: {.lesson-question}
**Guiding question:** What do we gain when we describe data as relations instead of as files, records, or screen layouts?
:::
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

1. use the terms **relation**, **attribute**, **tuple**, **domain**, **schema**, and **instance** precisely;
2. distinguish a relation from its tabular display;
3. explain the difference among a **superkey**, **candidate key**, **primary key**, and **foreign key**;
4. explain why the relational model separates logical description from physical storage; and
5. explain why a formal data model is useful even before we introduce a query language.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Keep one sentence in mind

The relational model gives us a language for describing **what data means** without committing to **how the data is stored or traversed**.
:::

## 1. Start with a shared vocabulary

We will use a small stream-monitoring example throughout the unit.

$$
\text{site}(\text{site\_id},\ \text{site\_code},\ \text{watershed},\ \text{reach\_name})
$$

$$
\text{observation}(\text{observation\_id},\ \text{site\_id},\ \text{observed\_at},\ \text{temperature\_c})
$$

Here is one possible instance of `site`:

| site_id | site_code | watershed | reach_name |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 101 | CC-01 | Clark Fork | Clear Creek Lower |
| 102 | BF-01 | Blackfoot | North Fork |
| 103 | RK-02 | Rock Creek | Ranch Bend |

Here is one possible instance of `observation`:

| observation_id | site_id | observed_at | temperature_c |
|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | 101 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 8.4 |
| 2 | 101 | 2026-05-01 10:00 | 9.1 |
| 3 | 102 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 7.8 |
| 4 | 101 | 2026-05-01 11:00 | 9.7 |

### The core terms

| Term | Clear definition | Example here |
|---|---|---|
| Relation | An abstract set of tuples over named attributes | `site` or `observation` |
| Attribute | A named component of a relation | `site_id`, `observed_at` |
| Tuple | One fact-record in the relation: one value for each attribute | `(2, 101, 2026-05-01 10:00, 9.1)` |
| Domain | The set of allowed or meaningful values for an attribute | Site codes such as `CC-01`; temperatures measured in degrees C |
| Schema | The relation name together with its attributes | `observation(observation_id, site_id, observed_at, temperature_c)` |
| Instance | The tuples currently present in the relation | The four displayed `observation` tuples |

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Schema and instance are different

The **schema** says what kind of facts may be stored. The **instance** says which facts are stored right now. A relation can have a schema even when its current instance is empty.
:::

### A relation is not the same thing as a grid on the screen

The displayed table is a convenient representation of a relation instance, but the relation itself is more abstract than its display.

- The relation does not depend on a particular column width, font, or interface.
- The relation does not depend on a particular file layout on disk.
- The relation does not inherently come with a row order.

For example, these two displays can represent the same relation instance:

| Run | Possible display order of `observation_id` values |
|---|---|
| First execution | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| Later execution | 3, 1, 4, 2 |

### Attributes have meaning, not just types

`site_id` and `observation_id` might both be stored as integers, but they do not mean the same thing. Likewise, a timestamp in `observed_at` has a different role from a timestamp in some hypothetical `reviewed_at` attribute, even if both use the same SQL type.

This is why the relational vocabulary matters. It encourages us to ask not only "what type is this value?" but also "what role does this attribute play in the relation?"

## 2. Keys identify tuples

When we say an attribute set is a key, we are making a statement about all valid instances of a relation, not just the sample currently on the screen.

### Key terminology

| Term | Definition | Example in this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Superkey | Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple | `{site_id}` or `{site_id, watershed}` in `site` |
| Candidate key | A minimal superkey | `{site_id}` and `{site_code}` in `site` |
| Primary key | The candidate key chosen as the main identifier | `site_id` in `site` |
| Foreign key | An attribute whose values must match a key in another relation | `observation.site_id` referencing `site.site_id` |

### A worked example: key versus superkey

In the `site` relation, suppose the course design intends both `site_id` and `site_code` to be unique for every site.

Then:

- `{site_id}` is a superkey because no two site tuples should share the same `site_id`.
- `{site_code}` is also a superkey because no two site tuples should share the same `site_code`.
- `{site_id, watershed}` is also a superkey, but it is not minimal.

Why is `{site_id, watershed}` not a candidate key? Because `site_id` by itself is already enough. Adding `watershed` does not help identify the tuple; it only makes the identifying set larger.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Minimality is the difference

A **candidate key** is not just unique. It is unique with no unnecessary attributes attached.
:::

### Additional example 1: a relation with multiple candidate keys

Consider a simple student relation:

$$
\text{student}(\text{student\_id},\ \text{netid},\ \text{university\_email},\ \text{display\_name})
$$

| student_id | netid | university_email | display_name |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 2001 | aria7 | aria7@umontana.edu | Aria Chen |
| 2002 | mateo3 | mateo3@umontana.edu | Mateo Ruiz |
| 2003 | priya11 | priya11@umontana.edu | Priya Shah |

If the institution guarantees that `student_id`, `netid`, and `university_email` are each unique, then all three are candidate keys.

- `{student_id}` is a candidate key.
- `{netid}` is a candidate key.
- `{university_email}` is a candidate key.
- `{student_id, display_name}` is a superkey, but not a candidate key, because `student_id` already suffices.
- `{display_name}` is not a superkey, because two students could share the same name.

If we choose `student_id` as the primary key, the other two candidate keys still matter. They remain alternate ways of identifying a student uniquely.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Class prompt:** Which of the following are superkeys for `student`: `{netid}`, `{display_name}`, `{student_id, netid}`, `{university_email, display_name}`? Which of those are candidate keys?
:::

### Additional example 2: a relation whose key is composite

Now consider course sections and enrollments:

$$
\text{section}(\text{section\_id},\ \text{course\_code},\ \text{term\_code},\ \text{section\_number})
$$

$$
\text{enrollment}(\text{student\_id},\ \text{section\_id},\ \text{enrolled\_on},\ \text{final\_letter\_grade})
$$

| section_id | course_code | term_code | section_number |
|---:|---|---|---:|
| 501 | CSCI340 | 2026FA | 1 |
| 502 | CSCI340 | 2026FA | 2 |
| 610 | MATH152 | 2026FA | 1 |

| student_id | section_id | enrolled_on | final_letter_grade |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 2001 | 501 | 2026-08-17 | A- |
| 2002 | 501 | 2026-08-17 | B+ |
| 2001 | 610 | 2026-08-18 | A |

In `enrollment`, no single attribute identifies a tuple by itself:

- `student_id` is not enough because one student can enroll in multiple sections.
- `section_id` is not enough because one section contains multiple students.
- `{student_id, section_id}` is a candidate key if the design allows at most one enrollment record per student per section.

This example is useful because it also makes foreign keys visible:

- `enrollment.student_id` is a foreign key referencing `student.student_id`.
- `enrollment.section_id` is a foreign key referencing `section.section_id`.

So `enrollment` is a good reminder that a relation can have:

- a composite primary key;
- multiple foreign keys; and
- attributes such as `enrolled_on` and `final_letter_grade` that describe the relationship rather than either entity alone.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Class prompt:** Why is `{student_id, section_id, enrolled_on}` a superkey but not a candidate key for `enrollment`? What real-world rule makes `{student_id, section_id}` work as a key?
:::

### What is not a key?

In the sample above, the attribute `watershed` is not a superkey. Multiple sites could belong to the Clark Fork watershed, so `watershed = 'Clark Fork'` does not identify one tuple uniquely.

Likewise, in `observation`, the fact that all four displayed timestamps happen to be different does **not** prove that `observed_at` is a candidate key. A future tuple could easily reuse a time:

| observation_id | site_id | observed_at | temperature_c |
|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 5 | 103 | 2026-05-01 10:00 | 11.2 |

Now two tuples share `observed_at = 2026-05-01 10:00`, so `observed_at` alone cannot identify an observation.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** In `observation`, is `{observation_id, site_id}` a candidate key or only a superkey? Explain your answer using minimality.
:::

## 3. Why this abstraction is useful

The vocabulary above is not academic decoration. It supports a practical goal: users and designers should be able to describe data and relationships without specifying one traversal strategy or one storage format.

### Before declarative query languages

Suppose observations are stored in records connected by pointers. To find warm readings from site `CC-01`, a program might be written to:

1. locate the record for `CC-01`;
2. follow its pointer to the first observation;
3. follow a linked list of later observations;
4. inspect each temperature; and
5. copy qualifying fields into an output record.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S["Site record<br/>CC-01"] --> O1["Observation<br/>08:00 · 7.9C"]
    O1 --> O2["Observation<br/>09:00 · 8.4C"]
    O2 --> O3["Observation<br/>10:00 · 9.1C"]
    O3 --> O4["Observation<br/>11:00 · 9.7C"]

    classDef record fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    class S,O1,O2,O3,O4 record;
```

That program may work, but notice what it assumes:

- where to begin;
- which links exist;
- how records are chained together; and
- how to traverse the storage structure.

If the storage design changes, the program may need to change even when the question stays the same.

### Separate the description of a question from one algorithm

Compare the pointer-following procedure above with this request:

> Return the time and temperature of observations from site `CC-01` whose temperature is at least 9C.

This request states the desired result, but it does not say whether the system should scan a file, use an index, follow pointers, process observations first, or process sites first.

::: {.concept-strip}
**Navigation-dependent request:** tied to one path through stored records<br>
**Logical request:** states what properties the desired answer must have
:::

That separation creates flexibility. The system can change storage structures or execution strategies without forcing the user to rewrite the meaning of the question.

## 4. A short history of the separation

Database systems did not become relational because earlier systems were foolish. They were built for different hardware and workload constraints. But one major shift was the move from navigation-dependent programs toward logical descriptions of data.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Application-specific files<br/>record layouts in programs"] --> B["Hierarchical and network systems<br/>predefined navigation paths"]
    B --> C["Relational model<br/>data described as relations"]
    C --> D["Formal query languages<br/>over relations"]
    D --> E["DBMS chooses storage and<br/>execution details"]

    classDef early fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef model fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef system fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A,B early;
    class C,D model;
    class E system;
```

In his 1970 paper, E. F. Codd proposed describing shared data using mathematical relations while insulating users from many internal representation details. The engineering goal was **data independence**: applications should depend more on the logical meaning of data than on a particular physical layout.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The formality serves an engineering purpose

Precise definitions let us say what a relation is, what counts as a key, what kinds of facts may be represented, and later, what a query means independently of one implementation.
:::

## 5. Put the ideas together

The lesson's logic is one chain:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Precise vocabulary<br/>for data"] --> B["Keys identify tuples<br/>across valid instances"]
    B --> C["Relations describe facts<br/>and relationships"]
    C --> D["Logical meaning stays stable<br/>when storage changes"]
    D --> E["Formal query languages become possible"]

    classDef problem fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef idea fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef outcome fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A,B problem;
    class C,D idea;
    class E outcome;
```

::: {.takeaway-panel}
## The main claim

The relational model sounds mathematical because it is trying to be exact about data. That exactness is what lets us describe information and relationships in a way that survives changes in storage layout and execution strategy.
:::

## Looking ahead

Next, we will use **relational algebra** as a formal language for expressing questions over relations. The point will not be to guess one traversal algorithm, but to describe the logical operations that define the answer.
